items.text: Bahrain said an Iranian attack late Saturday hit a civilian industrial facility and set it on fire; no one was hurt.
items.detail: Bahrain's Interior Ministry did not name the site; residents told AFP they saw smoke over Sitra Island, home to state oil company Bapco's refinery. The Bahrain Defence Force said air defenses intercepted several Iranian attacks and that falling shrapnel caused damage but no casualties. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they fired missiles and drones at U.S. positions at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in retaliation for U.S. drone flights over Iran, and claimed two Patriot radars were hit; U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond. Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet and has reported several Iranian attacks this week after a lull of several weeks.
items.why: Iran is again striking a Gulf ally that hosts a major U.S. base, widening the war beyond the Strait of Hormuz.

items.text: A Russian drone collapsed much of a five-story apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, early Sunday; at least 14 people may be trapped, Zelenskyy said.
items.detail: Ukraine's State Emergency Service said the strike destroyed apartments from the ground to the upper floors; rescuers evacuated nine people, including a child, and a teenager was hospitalized with shrapnel wounds. Kyiv regional chief Tymur Tkachenko said the blast also damaged a kindergarten and a shop. The search of the rubble was continuing.
items.why: Russia's strikes on homes are continuing even as U.S.-led peace talks go on.

items.text: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, the cartel boss called "El Chapo Isidro" and one of the FBI's 10 most wanted, was captured in Mexico, officials confirmed Saturday.
items.detail: Mexico's security chief said Saturday morning that army and National Guard special forces captured Meza Flores and two other leaders of his organization Friday night in Guasave, Sinaloa, in an operation the defense ministry said was coordinated with U.S. intelligence. He was flown to Mexico City to face prosecutors; Mexico says he faces a U.S. extradition order on drug-trafficking charges. The U.S. offered up to $5 million for him and says his group smuggled heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana into the United States for more than 20 years. The raid set off firefights and burning roadblocks across northern Sinaloa; Mexico's Defense Cabinet said Saturday afternoon that seven suspected cartel gunmen and four soldiers were killed.
items.why: It removes one of the top suppliers of drugs to the U.S. as Washington presses Mexico to act against the cartels.

items.text: U.S. Central Command denied Saturday an Iranian claim that Iran's air defenses hit a U.S. F-16 over the Gulf and forced it to make an emergency landing.
items.detail: Iranian state media said air defenses targeted the jet Friday evening, causing it to abort its mission and land at a nearby airport. "Iran did not attack a US F-16 fighter aircraft yesterday — at all," Central Command said, adding that all U.S. fighter jets in the Middle East were safe and accounted for. Iran has made similar claims during the war that the U.S. military has denied.
items.why: Competing claims about attacks on U.S. aircraft come as tankers keep getting hit near the Strait of Hormuz.

items.text: Polish prosecutors confirmed Saturday that a missile that crashed in Poland was a Russian Kh-101 built this year, as NATO's chief vowed to defend "every inch" of Polish territory.
items.detail: Investigators in Lublin said propulsion and guidance parts recovered at Nowy Lipowiec, about 60 km from the Ukrainian border, came from a Russian-made missile manufactured in the fourth quarter of 2026; work continues at the other two crash sites. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte met Prime Minister Donald Tusk in Warsaw, called the incursion "clearly dangerous" and said NATO commanders are assessing deterrence and defense. Poland has asked for more NATO support on the eastern flank but has not invoked Article 4 consultations. No one was hurt; Russia has not commented.
items.why: Confirmation that Russian weapons hit NATO soil raises pressure on the alliance to respond.

items.text: A Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad, the Sparta II, caught fire after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland Saturday; Finland's military said Ukraine was likely behind it.
items.detail: Finland's coast guard was alerted at about 8:50 a.m. local time (1:50 a.m. ET), about 50 km west of Suursaari island; the burning ship drifted into Finnish waters and its crew was evacuated to a Russian vessel. Kaliningrad's governor said two drones were used. The ship, run by a company tied to Russia's defense ministry, is under U.S. and Ukrainian sanctions. Finland set temporary air and sea restrictions and said a Russian helicopter may have violated its airspace. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said "war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity." Kyiv has not commented. No environmental damage was found.
items.why: The strike brings the war into busy Baltic shipping lanes next to NATO members.

items.text: Two more tankers leaving the Strait of Hormuz were hit by unidentified projectiles off Oman early Saturday, less than an hour apart, the British navy's UKMTO center said.
items.detail: The first tanker was struck on its stern about 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at about 0500 GMT (midnight ET); about 50 minutes later a second outbound tanker was hit in its engine room about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab. No one was reported hurt, and any environmental damage was not yet known, UKMTO said. The attacks follow Friday's strike that set a tanker on fire about 8 nautical miles north of Khasab. The ships were not named.
items.why: Strikes on ships in the strait, which carried about a fifth of the world's oil before the war, keep oil prices and the Iran war on edge.

week.text: The S&P 500 and the Dow both fell into a correction Friday, more than 10% below their record highs, as the AI stock sell-off deepened.
week.detail: By preliminary closing figures, the S&P 500 fell 3.59% to 6,918.45, its seventh straight loss and longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq dropped 5.13% to 22,654.15 and turned negative for 2026, and the Dow lost 1.85% to 48,188.18. All three had their worst week since April 2025. Nvidia fell about 14% and Micron about 14%; Anthropic's shares posted a steep loss on their second day of trading. Bitcoin dropped below $60,000. Traders are pricing a near-certain quarter-point Fed rate hike in December.
week.why: The slide hits the 401(k)s and retirement savings of tens of millions of Americans, and it came a day after Anthropic's record IPO failed to steady AI shares.

week.text: Anthropic's stock closed its first trading day about 17% above its $83 IPO price, but the wider market fell about 2% as AI shares slid.
week.detail: Anthropic opened at $111.50 shortly before noon, briefly valuing the company above $2 trillion and topping $115, before fading to close near $97. The S&P 500 erased an early 1.3% gain and fell about 2% for a sixth straight loss, its longest losing streak since April 2024; the Dow fell about 1,100 points (2.2%) to back below 50,000 and the Nasdaq lost about 2.3%. AMD dropped about 10% after investigative outlet Hunterbrook disclosed a short position citing its China dealings; AMD denied wrongdoing.
week.why: The record IPO was seen as a test of investor faith in AI, and it did not stop a weeks-long slide in tech stocks.

week.text: Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, the U.N.'s top court ruled Thursday, the first time it has found a country itself responsible for genocide.
week.detail: The International Court of Justice found that Myanmar's security forces intentionally killed Rohingya, caused them serious bodily or mental harm and imposed measures meant to prevent births during the 2017 "clearance operations" in northern Rakhine state, and that Myanmar failed to prevent and punish genocide. The court cited an estimated 10,000 Rohingya killed; about 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. It ordered Myanmar to investigate and prosecute those responsible, allow safe return of displaced Rohingya, and compensate them, with the amount to be set later; Myanmar must report back within two years. The judgment in the case brought by The Gambia in 2019 is final, binding and without appeal. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres welcomed it.
week.why: It is the first time the world court has held a state directly responsible for committing genocide.
